extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of dramatic theory / literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic poetry (drama), especially plot, character, discovery, and performance elements that produce the tragic effects of pity and terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excite pity and terror
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper object of tragedy is to excite pity and terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These passions should be produced preferably by the combination of incidents (the fable) rather than by mere representation. If the spectacle alone produces horror without the incidents, the work lacks the properties of tragedy. Examples: a fable so constituted that merely hearing the incidents would cause shuddering and compassion; anti-pattern: relying on stage horror (sight) rather than incident-combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero's moral standing (medium character)
rubrics_metrics.description: The person represented should be neither eminently virtuous nor conspicuously wicked, but a medium — a man in high reputation and prosperity who suffers from some error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pity is excited by misfortunes of the undeserving; terror by misfortunes of those equal to us. A very wicked person falling from happiness to misery excites neither pity nor terror. Prefer a character of high repute who errs (examples: Oedipus, Thyestes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple (single) fable preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: A fable properly constructed should be simple rather than double, and the change should be from happiness to misery (not the reverse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The change ought not to be due to wickedness but to some great error. Best tragedies often derive subjects from a few families with terrifying events (Alcmeon, Oedipus, Thyestes). Anti-pattern: double/composite fables that split focus or end with reconciliation like comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility and limits of double composition
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another form having a double composition (different catastrophe for virtuous and vicious) which some prefer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form sometimes gratifies weaker spectators but the satisfaction resembles comedy, not true tragedy. The poet should be aware that composing for audience gratification can compromise tragic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of tragic effect: incidents not merely representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity and terror should arise from the actions themselves; the fable ought to be so constituted that hearing the incidents would produce the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To effect these effects by means of spectacle alone is unskilful and more the business of the theatre manager. Examples of bad practice: introducing hordes of horrid figures to frighten the audience (Aeschylus' Eumenides considered excessive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate relational contexts for tragic actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions producing pity must happen between persons who are dear to each other (friends, relatives); actions between enemies or indifferent persons produce little pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: brother killing brother, son and father, mother and son. If one enemy kills another, pity is only from the sufferer's distress. Select incidents where misfortune befalls those with close ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to invent vs. respect for received stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may invent fables and arrange circumstances of received stories with propriety, but should not frivolously deviate from strongly established traditional plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain received stories (e.g., Clytemnestra killed by Orestes) should not be altered lightly; yet the poet's office includes inventing and arranging fables properly. Use judgement when altering well-known traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of action regarding knowledge and agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Four possible forms for how an action and its knowledge are arranged: (1) performed knowingly, (2) performed ignorantly with discovery after, (3) person intends but does not act, (4) about to act through ignorance and discovery occurs before acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of these, acting ignorantly with discovery afterwards is best (e.g., Oedipus); intending but not acting is worst (odious because of wicked intention without tragic suffering). Examples illustrate each form (Medea, Hæmon, Oedipus, Merope/Helle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of recognition/discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forms of discovery include by tokens (natural or adventitious), poet-invented proofs (artificial/inartificial), recollection or sight, reasoning (syllogism), and false reasoning of spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discoveries derived from the incidents themselves and arising from probable means are best (examples: Oedipus, Iphigenia). Next best are syllogistic inferences. Avoid contrived poet-invented devices (letters, arbitrary tokens) which border on inartificial contrivances; prefer discoveries that are intrinsic and probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inartificial tokens and contrivances
rubrics_metrics.description: Discoveries effected by arbitrary poetical contrivances (letters, convenient jewels, unrelated tokens) are inartificial and less meritorious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: Odysseus discovered by natural scar (more meritorious) versus discovery by a letter or invented shuttle that owes more to the poet's mouth than the fable. Use tokens only when they arise plausibly from the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners / character construction — moral goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: In forming the manners (character), the first and most essential thing is that they should be good (morally good).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manners will be evident from dialogue or action; even lower-status characters (women, slaves) may be shown as good. Aristotle links 'good' to being esteemed by good persons (example: Ulysses by Minerva, Achilles by Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners — be in character
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners should be 'in character' — actions and speech must fit the kind of person being represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a distinction between general moral goodness and the particular traits of a character (e.g., Achilles, Ulysses). Avoid behaviours that are out of character for the role portrayed (Menelaus in Orestes cited as an example of bad introduction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners — consistency of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be consistent; if an inconsistent person is drawn, the inconsistency itself must be consistently presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inconsistent character should not be made inconsistent in some scenes and consistent in others without justification. Anti-pattern: Iphigenia in Aulis criticized for inconsistent behavior; but a character may be managed to make apparent irregularities cohere with foundational traits if done persuasively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and probability in manners and incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity and probability should be observed both in manners and in the progression of incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unravelling of the plot should arise from the fable itself, not from external machinery (deus ex machina). Admit no circumstance contrary to reason among incidents except where the status of the drama (e.g., divine agency) justifies it; prefer probable, necessary causes for actions and discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's imaginative empathy and viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should consider everything as passing before his eyes and enter as much as possible into the spirit of the subject undertaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being moved by the passions oneself helps express them naturally and affect others; the poet's imaginative presence facilitates choosing what is proper in performance (example: poet's eye, Shakespeare citation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition order: fable first, episodes after
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether using known stories or inventing new ones, first form the fable generally, then insert episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes must be connected to the fable and concise; in drama episodes are subordinate and should not bloat the work as in epic. Example: Iphigenia narrative: core fable then addition of episodes like madness of Orestes that serve the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot vs solution — definition and centrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish plot and solution: the plot comprises events up to the turning/point of fortune; the solution comprises what passes from the commencement of the change of fortune to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a tragedy by its plot and solution rather than merely by its fable. Many fail by composing good plots but bad solutions; the poet should be equally skilful in both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of tragedy and aims
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four species of tragedy: the complex (depending on peripeteia and discovery), the pathetic, the moral (ethical), and the simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should strive to excel in as many of these forms as possible, prioritizing those most esteemed by the audience and critics. Be mindful that audiences may expect excellence across forms but specialization is also recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epic-like multiplicity of fables
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should not take the form of an epic containing many separate fables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to represent an extensive action (e.g., the whole destruction of Troy) in one tragedy leads to failure or unfavourable reception; divide large narratives into parts rather than compressing all into one play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted use of wonderful means within probability
rubrics_metrics.description: In tragedies that depend on peripeteia and a single action, poets sometimes use means that appear wonderful but are agreeable and not contrary to probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable for many things that seem improbable to happen, provided they are acceptable to the feelings of the audience. Examples cited include a wise but wicked man being deceived, or a brave unjust man vanquished — agreeable to feelings and not necessarily contrary to probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as an actor contributing to action
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus ought to be considered as one of the actors and should contribute to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chorus should not be used in the manner of Euripides (where sung parts often lack relation to the fable), but rather like Sophocles, with songs and interventions that advance or integrate with the drama. Avoid embolima (musical insertions) that are unrelated to the subject or impede plot cohesion.
